plan: SAT R&W batch 68: 9 new items on new passages CLD-P-SAT-RW-000608..000616 (Zheng He WIC, Hokule'a inference, quiz-score quantitative evidence, Cahokia cross-text, Franklin Gulf Stream purpose, Krakatoa boundary, Dust Bowl whom, Harriet Tubman transition, Lowell mills synthesis). Topics checked against every bank and the combined bank. Plus S067-03 and S067-06 resubmitted as revision 2 on their previously unbanked passages. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: How big were the ships?
passages.text: Between 1405 and 1433, the Chinese admiral Zheng He led seven great fleets across the Indian Ocean. Some Ming-era accounts describe his largest "treasure ships" as more than 400 feet long, but many historians consider those figures ______: no remains of ships that size have been found, and a wooden hull so long would have been very difficult to keep seaworthy.

passages.title: Steering by stars
passages.text: Some scholars once argued that the remote islands of the Pacific were settled mostly by accident, as canoes drifted off course. In 1976, the double-hulled voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed about 2,500 miles from Hawaii to Tahiti. Its navigator, Mau Piailug, used the stars, ocean swells, and the flight of birds, without any instruments. This voyage suggests that ______

passages.title: Lunch and learning
passages.text:
A student compared average quiz scores in two classes before and after a school moved lunch earlier in the day.
Class A: before 74, after 75
Class B: before 70, after 79
The student claims that the schedule change was followed by a much larger improvement in class B than in class A.

passages.title: The fall of a city
passages.text:
Text 1
Cahokia, a large city built by Mississippian people near present-day St. Louis, was largely abandoned by about 1350. One widely repeated explanation held that residents cut down the surrounding forests for fuel and building, causing erosion and floods that ruined the city's farmland.

Text 2
In 2021, a team led by archaeologist Caitlin Rankin examined soil layers beneath one of Cahokia's earthen mounds. They found no layers of flood sediment from the period when the city was occupied, and the ground surface remained stable until well after people had left.

passages.title: Slow mail
passages.text: In the 1760s, Benjamin Franklin, then a deputy postmaster for the British colonies, wondered why mail ships from England took about two weeks longer to cross the Atlantic than many merchant ships. His cousin Timothy Folger, a whaling captain, explained that American sailors knew of a strong current flowing east and avoided sailing against it, while the mail ships' captains did not. Franklin later had a chart of the current, which he called the Gulf Stream, printed for sea captains.

passages.title: Red skies
passages.text: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa, a volcanic island in what is now Indonesia, had effects that reached far beyond the ______ fine ash thrown into the upper atmosphere produced vividly colored sunsets around the world for months afterward.

passages.title: Leaving the Plains
passages.text: Years of drought and dust storms during the 1930s drove many families off their farms. By 1940, roughly 2.5 million people had moved out of the Plains states, many of ______ headed west to California in search of work.

passages.title: More than one role
passages.text: Harriet Tubman is best known for guiding enslaved people to freedom along the Underground Railroad. ______ during the Civil War she served the Union Army as a scout and spy, and in 1863 she helped lead a raid along South Carolina's Combahee River that freed more than 700 people.

passages.title: Notes on the mills
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In the 1830s and 1840s, the textile mills of Lowell, Massachusetts, employed thousands of young women.
- Workers commonly labored about 12 to 13 hours a day.
- From 1840 to 1845, workers published The Lowell Offering, a magazine of their own writing.
- In 1834, workers walked out to protest a cut in wages.
- In 1836, workers walked out again to protest higher charges for company boardinghouses.

passages.title: Feeder visits
passages.text:
A student counted the birds that visited a feeder in the hour after sunrise on four mornings. On two mornings the feeder held sunflower seed, and on two it held millet.
Sunflower: 34 visits and 30 visits
Millet: 12 visits and 16 visits
The student claims that the birds strongly preferred sunflower seed to millet.

passages.title: Poems for passengers
passages.text: After high school, Paul Laurence Dunbar, the son of formerly enslaved parents, ran the single elevator in an office building in Dayton, Ohio. He wrote poems between trips and in 1893 paid to have his first collection, Oak and Ivy, printed. The ______ passengers became some of his first readers, buying copies for a dollar each.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: no remains of ships that size have been found
candidates.explanation: Historians doubt the figures because no such ships have been found and they would have been hard to keep seaworthy, so they consider the figures "exaggerated."

B.rationale: The text gives reasons to doubt the figures, not to confirm them.

C.rationale: Over 400 feet would be enormous, not modest.

D.rationale: The accounts are from the Ming era; their age is not the issue.

hints: Do the historians trust the figures?
candidates.remember: Use the evidence after the colon to infer the historians' view.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: most Pacific islands were settled by sailors from Tahiti.
choices.B: accidental drifting could not have carried any canoe to a distant island.
choices.C: early Pacific sailors could navigate long distances on purpose.
choices.D: modern instruments are less accurate than traditional navigation.

candidates.explanation: A successful 2,500-mile voyage using only traditional cues shows that deliberate navigation, not just accidental drifting, could explain how distant islands were reached.

A.rationale: The text does not say where most settlers came from.

B.rationale: The voyage shows deliberate navigation was possible, not that drifting was impossible.

D.rationale: The voyage used no instruments and makes no comparison of accuracy.

hints: What earlier view does the voyage challenge?

strategy.explanation: Connect the evidence to the view in the first sentence.

candidates.remember: An inference should be no stronger than the evidence.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the student's claim?

choices.A: Class B's average after the change was 79, higher than class A's 75.
choices.B: Class A's average was higher than class B's before the change.
choices.C: Both classes had higher averages after the change than before it.
choices.D: Class B's average rose 9 points; class A's rose only 1 point.

candidates.evidence: a much larger improvement in class B than in class A
candidates.explanation: The improvements are 79 − 70 = 9 for class B and 75 − 74 = 1 for class A, which supports the claim.

A.rationale: This compares the after scores, not the size of each class's improvement.

B.rationale: This describes the starting scores, not the improvements.

C.rationale: This is true but does not compare the sizes of the improvements.

hints: What does "improvement" require you to compute?
candidates.remember: Support a claim about change with the changes themselves.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would Rankin's team (Text 2) most likely respond to the explanation described in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that deforestation caused floods but placing them after the city was abandoned
choices.B: By noting that the soil evidence shows no sign of the floods that explanation requires
choices.C: By arguing that Cahokia was never as large as Text 1 suggests
choices.D: By proving that drought, not flooding, caused residents to leave

candidates.evidence: They found no layers of flood sediment
candidates.explanation: The explanation depends on floods during occupation; Text 2 finds no flood sediment from that period, so the team would say the evidence does not support it.

A.rationale: Text 2 finds no flood layers during occupation, which undercuts the explanation rather than agreeing with it.

C.rationale: Text 2 does not discuss the city's size.

D.rationale: Text 2 does not identify any cause of abandonment.

hints: What does the Text 1 explanation require?

strategy.explanation: Compare the explanation's prediction with the finding.

candidates.remember: A finding can undercut an explanation by contradicting what it predicts.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To argue that merchant captains were better sailors than British naval officers
choices.B: To explain how whaling captains located whales in the Atlantic Ocean
choices.C: To describe the delays that British mail faced on land in the colonies
choices.D: To show how a practical question led to a chart of an ocean current

candidates.evidence: Franklin later had a chart of the current
candidates.explanation: The text moves from Franklin's question about slow mail ships, to Folger's explanation of the current, to the chart Franklin had printed.

A.rationale: The text explains a difference in route knowledge, not general skill.

B.rationale: The text does not discuss locating whales.

C.rationale: The delays discussed were at sea, not on land.

hints: How does the text begin, and how does it end?
candidates.remember: A purpose answer should cover the whole text.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: fine ash thrown into the upper atmosphere produced vividly colored sunsets
candidates.explanation: Both parts are independent clauses, so a semicolon correctly joins them.

A.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

B.rationale: Without punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

D.rationale: The comma after "and" wrongly separates the conjunction from its clause.

strategy.explanation: Find where the first clause ends.

candidates.remember: Join independent clauses with a semicolon or a period.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: roughly 2.5 million people had moved out of the Plains states
candidates.explanation: "Many of whom headed west" is a dependent clause that refers to the people; "whom" is the object of "of."

A.rationale: "Many of them headed west" is an independent clause joined with only a comma, creating a comma splice.

B.rationale: After the preposition "of," the object form "whom" is needed.

C.rationale: "Which" refers to things, not to people.

hints: Is the pronoun the object of "of"?

strategy.explanation: Test each choice for case and sentence structure.

candidates.remember: Use "whom" after a preposition in a relative clause.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: she served the Union Army as a scout and spy
candidates.explanation: The second sentence adds another role to the one for which she is best known, so an additive transition fits.

A.rationale: Her Civil War service did not replace her work on the Underground Railroad.

C.rationale: Her Underground Railroad work did not cause her army service.

D.rationale: Her Civil War service is not an example of guiding people on the Underground Railroad.

hints: Does the second sentence add, contrast, or illustrate?
candidates.remember: Use "In addition" to add a further point.

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize that the Lowell mill workers organized to protest their conditions. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: From 1840 to 1845, Lowell mill workers published The Lowell Offering, a magazine of their own writing.
choices.B: The textile mills of Lowell, Massachusetts, employed thousands of young women in the 1830s and 1840s.
choices.C: Lowell mill workers walked out in 1834 over a wage cut and again in 1836 over higher boardinghouse charges.
choices.D: Workers in the Lowell mills commonly labored about 12 to 13 hours a day.

candidates.evidence: workers walked out to protest a cut in wages
candidates.explanation: Only choice A describes the workers' organized walkouts against their conditions.

A.rationale: This shows a shared project, not a protest of conditions.

B.rationale: This gives background but does not mention any protest.

D.rationale: This describes a condition but not any organized response to it.

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against the goal.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must accomplish the stated goal.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the student's claim?

choices.A: Each sunflower morning had nearly twice or more the visits of either millet morning.
choices.B: The feeder received 34 visits on the first sunflower morning, its highest total.
choices.C: Visits on the two millet mornings differed by 4.
choices.D: The feeder received 92 visits in all across the four mornings.

candidates.evidence: the birds strongly preferred sunflower seed to millet
candidates.explanation: Each sunflower morning (34, 30) had roughly twice as many visits as either millet morning (12, 16), which supports a strong preference.

B.rationale: A single morning cannot show a preference.

C.rationale: This compares millet mornings with each other, not the two seeds.

D.rationale: A total does not compare the two seeds.

hints: What comparison does the claim require?

strategy.explanation: Compare the two kinds of seed directly.

candidates.remember: Support a comparison with data from both groups.

revision_history.reason: blind solver: "about twice" understated the 34 vs 12 comparison
revision_history.change: key reworded to "nearly twice or more"

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: ran the single elevator in an office building
candidates.explanation: The passengers belonged to one elevator, the one Dunbar operated, so the singular possessive "elevator's" is correct.

B.rationale: The plural possessive refers to more than one elevator, but Dunbar operated one.

C.rationale: A plural noun without an apostrophe cannot show possession here.

D.rationale: "Elevators's" is not a correct possessive form.

strategy.explanation: Decide singular or plural, then possessive.

revision_history.reason: blind solver: only weak contextual cue that one elevator was meant
revision_history.change: passage now says he ran the single elevator in an office building
